title: Freya and the Portrait
premise: Mirabel Lockridge, a night-shift dispatcher who has spent years listening to strangers' last rides, receives a confession letter for the murder of her estranged aunt Freya — postmarked the day after the funeral. The letter claims Freya's death was justice for a crime committed thirty years ago, when three teenagers covered up a drowning at a lakeside estate, and names Mirabel's late mother as an accomplice. As Mirabel traces alibis through old taxi logs, faded photographs, and witnesses who have built respectable lives on lies, she realizes the confessor is dying and wants the truth on record before it dies with them. In the end, Mirabel must choose between handing the evidence to police and letting a dying person's final act of justice stand — and discovers the confessor is someone whose voice she has heard every night on her radio.
about_author: Yara Oyelaran is a former emergency dispatcher turned novelist who writes mysteries about the people who answer phones in the dark. She lives near a lake that freezes early and keeps its secrets longer.

chapters.title: The Last Fare
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A routine night shift ends with news of Aunt Freya's death and a funeral invitation Mirabel almost ignores. Establishes her numb competence and distance from family. Emotional beat: grief she doesn't yet know how to feel.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At the funeral, distant relatives circle the will; afterward Mirabel finds a typed confession letter admitting to killing Freya, mailed the day after she died. She nearly throws it away, then reads the name of her mother. Beat: dread replacing grief.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibi
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The letter references a drowning at Harrow Lake, summer 1994, and three names: her mother, Freya, and an initial 'D.' Mirabel digs out her mother's boxes after the wake. Beat: the past cracking open like ice.

chapters.title: What the Dispatcher Hears
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, interwoven with dispatch calls. A caller asks about 'the Lockridge house' on the taxi line — someone knows she has the letter. First hint of surveillance. Beat: fear entering the safe space of work.

chapters.title: Harrow Lake
chapters.summary: Mirabel travels to the shuttered estate town. POV alternates briefly with a 1994 flashback chapter-voice: a boy named Danny sinking under the water while three figures watch from the dock. Beat: horror rendered quiet.

chapters.title: The Respectable Mr. Devane
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She finds 'D' — Douglas Devane, now a beloved retired judge. He is charming, grieving publicly for Freya, and lying smoothly about the summer of 1994. Beat: the sickening discovery that guilt wears a good suit.

chapters.title: Freya's Locked Room
chapters.summary: Mirabel breaks into Freya's sealed cottage and finds newspaper clippings, a second letter half-written to Mirabel, and a photograph of four teenagers — one face scratched out. Beat: Freya was investigating too, and died mid-sentence.

chapters.title: Tail Lights
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Someone follows her taxi back from the lake; she loses them using routes only a dispatcher would know. She realizes her professional skill is now survival. Beat: adrenaline and resolve hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Fourth Face
chapters.summary: Mirabel identifies the scratched-out figure as her mother, Ruth. A 1994 flashback shows Ruth begging the others to call for help and being silenced. Beat: love and betrayal colliding — her mother was both victim and accomplice.

chapters.title: A Dying Man's Confession
chapters.summary: Anonymous note leads Mirabel to a hospice where a terminally ill man, Eddie Marsh, once the estate caretaker's son, admits he saw everything and wrote the confession letter — but swears he didn't kill Freya. Beat: relief and confusion; the real killer still walks.

chapters.title: Judge and Jury
chapters.summary: Mirabel confronts Devane with Eddie's testimony. He threatens her with her mother's complicity, revealing Ruth took money for silence and drank herself to death over it. Beat: the price of survival made explicit and personal.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Her dispatch line receives a call from a number tied to Freya's cottage — silence, then breathing, then a click. Someone is taunting her through the one channel she trusts. Beat: paranoia tightening like a wire.

chapters.title: The Taxi Logs
chapters.summary: Mirabel cross-references thirty-year-old company logs with Freya's clippings and finds a fare record: the night Danny drowned, a cab was called to Harrow Lake and paid in cash by a woman — not any of the three teens. Beat: the case pivots; there was a fourth adult.

chapters.title: Miss Aldous Remembers
chapters.summary: Mirabel tracks down the former housekeeper, Vera Aldous, who reveals Danny was the Devanes' chauffeur's son and that Judge Devane's father orchestrated the cover-up — and that young Douglas drove the car. Beat: generational rot exposed.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Mirabel returns to find Freya's cottage ablaze. She saves the half-written letter but loses the photograph. Fire marshal calls it electrical; Mirabel knows better. Beat: the enemy escalating from watching to destroying.

chapters.title: Allies in the Dark
chapters.summary: Eddie, moved from his hospice bed by conscience, gives Mirabel his full written account and a key Freya mailed him before dying. Beat: fragile alliance; two damaged people choosing truth over safety.

chapters.title: The Key
chapters.summary: The key opens a deposit box containing Freya's complete dossier: Devane's fingerprints on the boat oar, kept by a bribed coroner, plus proof the coroner is now Devane's brother-in-law. Beat: the trap assembling piece by piece.

chapters.title: Invitation to Harrow Lake
chapters.summary: Devane calls Mirabel directly, offering money and her mother's cleaned-up legacy in exchange for the dossier — and subtly threatening Eddie's hospice. Beat: temptation and menace braided together; the point of no return.

chapters.title: Night Shift
chapters.summary: Mirabel uses the dispatch network to coordinate a plan: recording Devane's threats via the taxi line, staging a pickup at Harrow Lake. Flashback interlude: 15-year-old Ruth running along the shore, screaming a name no one answered. Beat: past and present converging on the same water.

chapters.title: The Dock at Midnight
chapters.summary: Climax. Mirabel lures Devane to the frozen dock wearing a wire; he confesses to killing Freya when she blackmailed him with the oar evidence, then tries to force Mirabel through the ice. Eddie arrives; Devane falls through and Mirabel must choose to save him. She does — because justice needs him alive. Beat: terror, choice, moral clarity.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Fallout. The recording convicts Devane despite the corrupted coroner; Eddie dies peacefully days later, his confession read aloud in court. Mirabel learns the taunting phone calls were Freya herself, alive long enough to guard her own investigation — the postmark was her final misdirection. Beat: grief transfigured into understanding.

chapters.title: Freya and the Portrait
chapters.summary: Resolution. Among Freya's effects, Mirabel finds the restored portrait of the four teenagers, her mother's face unscratched, with a note: 'Tell her story true.' Mirabel takes a new job training young dispatchers and scatters Freya's ashes at Harrow Lake in spring. Beat: quiet peace; identity reclaimed from the price of survival.
